analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act penalties on people without insurance and large employers that don't offer coverage.
analysis.headline: Introduced on the first day of the 115th Congress and backed by 12 cosponsors, all Republicans, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate two Affordable Care Act tax penalties: the individual mandate penalty on people who do not buy health insurance, and the employer mandate penalty on companies with 50 or more full-time workers that do not offer coverage. It would also erase the annual reporting rules tied to the employer mandate, and both repeals would apply starting in 2014, the year the rules took effect.
analysis.who_benefits: People who do not buy insurance would no longer owe the individual mandate penalty. Large employers with 50 or more full-time workers would avoid the per-employee penalties for not offering coverage and the paperwork that comes with proving they do, and some could save money by dropping or trimming coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate tax penalty, so people who choose not to buy health insurance would no longer owe a federal penalty.
Repeals the employer mandate, freeing employers with 50 or more full-time workers from penalties for not providing coverage and from the annual reporting requirement on what coverage they offer.
Makes both repeals retroactive to January 2014, the month the mandate rules took effect, which would mean penalties already collected could be refunded.

analysis.who_pays: The individual mandate works by keeping healthy people in the insurance pool; without it, healthier people have less reason to buy coverage, so premiums rise for the people who still buy insurance. Workers at large firms that respond by dropping coverage could lose their employer insurance and end up buying on their own or going uninsured. The federal government would also forgo penalty revenue and owe refunds of penalties paid since 2014.

drawbacks.text: The individual mandate exists to keep healthy, cheap-to-insure people in the pool alongside sicker ones. With the penalty gone, healthier people have less reason to buy coverage, leaving a sicker and more expensive pool and pushing premiums up for everyone who still buys insurance on their own.

Without the employer mandate, large employers would be free to stop offering coverage. The affected workers would have to find their own insurance or go without it, and many would land in the individual market at higher prices.
The repeal applies retroactively to 2014, so the federal government would have to refund penalties people and employers already paid for years of compliance, adding to the fiscal cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but uneven: individuals avoid a tax penalty worth a few hundred to a few thousand dollars a year, while large employers avoid per-employee penalties that could add up to far more. The offsetting risk is that both repeals pull the legs out from under the insurance pool with nothing put in their place — premiums rise for people who keep buying coverage, and some workers lose employer coverage entirely. As written, the gains are certain and immediate for employers, while the costs land gradually on insurance buyers, and the retroactive effective date adds refund costs on top.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Turner of Ohio introduced the bill on January 4, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, joined by seven original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax law.
It eventually gathered 12 cosponsors, every one of them a Republican.
No further action ever appeared: the committee never reported the bill out and no floor vote was held before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died in committee, the Affordable Care Act's coverage rules and penalties stayed on the books, so people who buy their own insurance and workers whose employers could have cut coverage are better off that it failed. Large employers lost the chance to avoid the penalties and reporting requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on ACA coverage rules

for.name: Rep. Michael R. Turner
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the 115th Congress.

for.name: 12 of 236 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 12 cosponsors were Republicans, including original cosponsors Reps. Farenthold, Duncan of South Carolina, DesJarlais, McClintock, Mullin, Roe of Tennessee, and Rogers of Alabama.

against.name: Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out, held no markup or vote on it, and let it die there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat ever signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no voting record exists to measure the split.

industries.industry: Large employers (50 or more full-time workers)
industries.note: The employer mandate taxes large firms $2,000–$3,000 per full-time worker if they do not offer affordable coverage; repealing it lets firms shed that cost and the associated reporting. The savings for employers could come out of workers' health coverage, which the penalty exists to protect.

Losing the individual mandate shrinks the pool of healthy paying customers and raises the average cost of those who remain, destabilizing the individual market. Insurers could pick up some customers whose employers drop coverage, but with a weaker mandate the trade is likely a net loss.
